analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil and gas profits above a 'reasonable' level and uses the money for home heating aid.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced beyond committee referral, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007 without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a new tax on profits that oil and natural gas companies make above what a newly created federal board judged 'reasonable.' The tax rate would climb with how far profits exceeded that benchmark — up to 100% on profits more than 5% above the reasonable level. All of the money raised would be appropriated to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which helps low-income households pay heating and cooling bills. The bill went to two House committees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households that qualify for home energy assistance, since every dollar of the new tax would flow directly into the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program on top of its regular appropriations. During the 2005 energy price spikes that prompted the bill, heating and gasoline costs hit those budgets hardest. If the tax discouraged extreme profit-taking during price spikes, consumers generally could benefit as well.

how_it_helps.text: The bill appropriates amounts equivalent to all taxes collected under the windfall profit provision to the Secretary of Health and Human Services for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, in addition to that program's regular funding [S3].

The tax targets only profit above a 'reasonable profit' determined by an independent board: 50% of profit exceeding reasonable profit by up to 2%, 75% for the next band, and 100% of profit exceeding reasonable profit by more than 5% [S3].
Board members would be barred from having financial interests in any business whose profits they judged, an anti-capture provision [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and natural gas producers and sellers of petroleum products, who would pay the excise tax on profits above the board's benchmark. To the extent companies passed the tax through to prices, some cost could fall on consumers at the pump or the meter, though the tax applies only to profit judged excessive. The oil industry and its allies also argued — in the broader 2005 windfall-tax debate — that taxing profits can discourage investment in new supply, which could keep prices high.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and natural gas producers and refiners

drawbacks.text: The tax depends entirely on a three-member presidentially appointed 'Reasonable Profits Board' deciding what profit is reasonable for every sale, a highly subjective judgment that would invite years of litigation and could be shaped by whoever occupies the White House [S3].

A windfall profits tax can discourage oil and gas investment precisely when more supply is needed; critics of such taxes note that producers facing a tax on above-benchmark profit may slow output or shift sales abroad, potentially raising consumer prices rather than lowering them.

The United States tried a crude oil windfall profit tax from 1980 to 1987, and later analyses found it increased domestic dependence on foreign oil by discouraging domestic production — an experience opponents of the 2005 proposal cited against it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is clear and targeted: a dedicated, growing funding stream for home energy assistance for low-income households, paid for by the companies earning the largest profits during price spikes. The design is genuinely debatable — the 'reasonable profit' standard is subjective and board-dependent, and the historical windfall tax of the 1980s is widely judged to have backfired by curbing domestic production. A simpler surtax or a straightforward excess-profit rate would have avoided some of that. As drafted, the bill's promise to energy-burdened households outweighed those design risks, but its structure left it open to fair criticism.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means and Appropriations committees the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Paul Kanjorski, a Pennsylvania Democrat, introduced the bill on September 7, 2005, amid high energy prices following Hurricanes Katrina and Rita [S1,S2,S3].
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committee on Appropriations for the portions falling under their jurisdiction [S5].
That referral was the bill's only action of record. No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill received just one cosponsor [S4,S5].
The bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, with all unfinished bills expiring [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and natural gas companies, which kept all profits above the pre-2005 baseline untaxed, and low-income energy assistance programs, which never received the dedicated funding stream.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies kept their profits untaxed

for.name: Rep. Paul Kanjorski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote from September 2005 until the Congress ended

against.name: House Appropriations Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed the 2005 wave of windfall-profits tax proposals, arguing they would discourage energy investment and raise prices

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; its sponsor and sole cosponsor were both Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded [S4].

industries.industry: Oil and natural gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would tax up to 100% of their profits above a board-determined 'reasonable' level, falling hardest in high-price years when their profits spike. The industry argues such taxes reduce investment and ultimately consumer supply; the public benefit is the dedicated LIHEAP funding and the deterrent on extreme profit-taking.
State and local LIHEAP programs would receive a new, dedicated funding stream on top of annual appropriations to help low-income households pay energy bills.
